FINAL DESIGN DOCUMENT
====================================================================
Title: Using autocorrelation (ACF) analysis to identify the optimal cycle length P for CycleNet in time series forecasting
Status: Design-only deliverable (no execution performed)

====================================================================
1. OBJECTIVES AND HYPOTHESIS
====================================================================
Primary objective: Determine whether, and how reliably, sample autocorrelation analysis can select the cycle length P for CycleNet that produces the best (lowest) held-out forecast error, where "optimal cycle length" is *operationally defined* as the P minimising validation MSE/MAE.

The question decomposes into two coupled hypotheses that the design tests separately:
  H1 (detection): The dominant peak(s) of the sample autocorrelation function (ACF) recover the true dominant periodicity P* of a dataset. Validated against synthetic data with KNOWN P (unambiguous ground truth) and against benchmarks with documented seasonal periods.
  H2 (optimality): Running CycleNet with P = ACF-derived candidate yields held-out error that is statistically indistinguishable from (within a noise band of) the best P found by a full P-sweep, and is no worse than the default frequency-based P. Quantified via a P-sweep error curve plus a rank-correlation check that ACF magnitude order predicts error order.
  H3 (mechanism/ablation): The cycle module itself is what delivers the improvement (RCF-on vs RCF-off), so that attributing the result to a correctly chosen P is valid.

Success criteria (pre-registered, per dataset):
  S1. ACF-picked P equals the true P* on synthetic data in ≥ 95% of generated datasets.
  S2. ACF-picked P has validation MSE/MAE within the noise band (mean ± 1 SE over seeds) of the sweep argmin, AND beats or ties default-P with error reduction ≥ 1% on average.
  S3. Kendall's tau_b between (ACF magnitude at P) and (CycleNet error at P) is negative and significant at p<0.05, or at minimum the ACF-picked P is among the top-2 ranked candidates by error.
  S4. RCF-on beats RCF-off on the same data/horizon (isolating the value of the cycle module).

====================================================================
2. DATA SELECTION AND RATIONALE
====================================================================
Rationale: ACF-based detection is only meaningful when periodicity dominates any trend/irregular component, so we deliberately select (a) synthetic data with known ground-truth P, and (b) real benchmarks with documented seasonal periods.

2.1 Synthetic data (validates H1 unambiguously)
Generators (seeded, 10 replicates per configuration, ~2000–10000 points each, univariate):
  - Seasonal AR/pseudo-AR: x_t = c + Σ_j a_j·sin(2π·t/P_j + φ_j) + ε_t, noise levels ε ~ N(0, σ²) with SNR ∈ {2, 5, 10}.
  - Deterministic seasonal with trend: x_t = linear trend + seasonal + AR(2) noise.
  - Stochastic seasonal (SAR-like): x_t = φ·x_{t−P} + ε_t.
  Configurations with single period P ∈ {6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 168} (to span daily/weekly patterns) and double-period variants (e.g., P1=24 with P2=168) to test multiple-periodicity ranking.
Role: the ONLY place where "true P" is known exactly; isolates claim H1 from H2.

2.2 Real benchmark datasets (validates H2/H3)
  - ETTh1 (hourly): known daily P=24 and weekly P=168 periods → tests multi-period selection.
  - ETTm1 (15-min): 4 series, daily P=96 → cross-frequency check vs ETTh1.
  - Electricity (ECL, 321 series, hourly): daily 24 + weekly 168 → tests per-variate ACF pooling on a wide multivariate set.
  - Weather (21 series, 10-min): daily P=144.
  - M4 subset (daily/weekly/monthly/quarterly, univariate, many series): covers low-frequency periods (P=7 / 7 / 12 / 4) and gives a many-dataset aggregation for the rank-correlation check.
Optional external anchor: compare with reported CycleNet numbers from the paper for the same datasets/horizons to sanity-check our implementation.

2.3 Preprocessing & splits (identical for all configs to keep P as the only variable)
  - Remove NaNs/inf, no global normalisation before ACF (but use per-series standardisation for detection); for the model, apply per-variate standardisation (mean/std) as in the CycleNet pipeline.
  - Split: chronological 60/20/20 train/val/test (no random shuffle — respects temporal order). ACF computed on TRAIN segment only (avoids information leakage from test into the P choice).

====================================================================
3. FULL ACF DETECTION PROCEDURE
====================================================================
Goal: convert each series into a small ranked set of candidate cycle lengths, with a single per-dataset recommendation.

3.1 Preprocessing per series (train segment only)
  a) Detrend: subtract OLS linear trend (a quadratic variant as sensitivity check). This removes the trend that in real data can otherwise be the dominant low-frequency ACF mass.
  b) Variance stabilisation: optional log transform if variance grows with level (checked via coefficient of variation per block).
  c) Stationarity guard: first-difference if the Augmented-Dickey-Fuller-style check indicates strong non-stationarity persists after detrending; re-run ACF on the differenced series and report both (differencing preserves periodicity at lag P but adds a −1 at lag 1 and reduces low-lag mass, so we note this in interpretation).
  d) Centre to zero mean.

3.2 Sample ACF
  For lag k = 1..K (K = min(L_lookback, 200)):
      r_k = [ Σ_{t} (z_t − z̄)(z_{t+k} − z̄) ] / [ Σ_t (z_t − z̄)² ],  z = preprocessed series.
  Use the standard estimator with N_T − k terms; require sufficient overlap (skip series with fewer than ~4·max candidate points).

3.3 Significance band
  Under white-noise null, r_k ≈ N(0, 1/N_eff); 95% Bartlett band = ±1.96/√N_eff, N_eff = length of z.
  Practical threshold: r_k must exceed max(1.96/√N_eff, 0.15) to count as a candidate — this filters spurious small peaks while staying generous for noisy real data.

3.4 Candidate extraction (per series)
  A lag k* is a candidate if:
    (i)  r_{k*−1} < r_{k*} ≥ r_{k*+1}   (local maximum),
    (ii) r_{k*} above the threshold in 3.3,
    (iii) k* ≥ 2 (lag-1 structure is AR not periodicity).
  Fundamental period = the SMALLEST such k* (integer multiples reappear as secondary peaks). To avoid double counting harmonics, we de-duplicate lags that are integer multiples/divisors of a smaller strong candidate (keep the smaller, but record the multiple as a secondary ranked option). Ties within ±1 lag (e.g., 23 vs 24 from noise) are merged to the mean.

3.5 Aggregation across series and variates (dataset-level)
  Two complementary rankings per dataset:
   (a) Magnitude ranking: average per-lag r_k across all series/variates → mean ACF profile; extract candidates as in 3.4 on the mean profile.
   (b) Vote ranking: for each lag, count the fraction of series where that lag is a candidate; rank by vote fraction.
  Final candidate list = top-k (k=5) lags from (a), re-ranked by (b) to break magnitude-ties. The top-1 becomes the recommended P_ACF for that dataset. Report both rankings; disagreement (>1 position shift) flags a heterogeneous-period dataset (handled in §4.3 and §5).

3.6 Ground-truth recovery check (H1) on synthetic data
  P_ACF == true P* (or its smallest harmonic) per replicate; report recovery rate and the full candidate list to show how far the "true" P ranks when not top-1.

3.7 Optional cross-check (not part of the core answer)
  FFT periodogram peak as a one-line corroboration only; the answer is ACF-based by task definition.

====================================================================
4. CYCLENET SETUP
====================================================================
4.1 How P enters the model (Residual Cycle Forecasting, RCF)
  CycleNet (Lin et al., NeurIPS 2024) augments a backbone forecaster (e.g., a linear/DLinear head) with an RCF module that holds a LEARNABLE cycle token of length P shared across time steps (per variate for multivariate data). For time step t the model emits a cycle component ŷ^cycle_t = token[t mod P]; the backbone is trained on residuals y_t − ŷ^cycle_{t−P} (cycle-to-cycle differences); forecast = backbone residual output + cycle component. Consequences that constrain our design:
   - P must be a single fixed positive integer per dataset (one cycle token, one period). This is why §3 aggregates to one P per dataset rather than per series.
   - RCF needs the lag-P history within the receptive window: lookback L must satisfy L ≥ 2·P (else the model cannot reference the previous cycle for early in-window steps). With L=336 this caps P ≤ 168, which comfortably covers all daily/weekly periods in our data while ruling out unrealistically long P (e.g., yearly for hourly data).

4.2 Model protocol (fixed across all P variants so P is the ONLY variable)
  - Backbone: DLinear-style head (the CycleNet default) for a lean, CPU-friendly baseline; note that the same protocol generalises to any backbone.
  - Lookback L = 336; horizons H ∈ {96, 192, 336, 720} for ETT/ECL/Weather; {24, 48, 168} or the M4 short-term horizons for M4 subsets.
  - Optimiser: Adam, lr 1e-3 (cosine decay), batch 32, MSE loss, early stopping on validation loss (patience 10).
  - Data normalisation per variate (standardisation) identical across variants.
  - Seeds: 3 seeds minimum, up to 5 if budget allows, identical seeds across all P variants of the same dataset/horizon (enables paired tests).

4.3 P-sweep range (per dataset)
  Let p1 = top ACF candidate, p2..p5 = the rest. Sweep set = {max(1, p1−2)…p1+2} ∪ {p2..p5} ∪ {default P by data frequency} ∪ {known alternates, e.g., 24 AND 168 for hourly data}. Clamp any candidate P to ≤ L/2 (=168) to respect the L ≥ 2P RCF constraint. This yields ~8–12 P values per dataset. Rationale: the sweep builds the error-vs-P landscape on which "optimal" is operationally defined, and tests whether the ACF picks a point on/near its minimum.

4.4 Baselines and controls, each tied to a specific claim it isolates
  C1 — CycleNet(P_ACF) vs CycleNet(P_default): the core head-to-head for H2's "at least as good as convention". P_default = {24 hourly, 96 for 15-min, 144 for 10-min, 7 weekly, 12 monthly, 4 quarterly} (the paper's frequency heuristic).
  C2 — CycleNet(P) for every P in the sweep: the error-vs-P curve; isolates H2's "optimality" (is P_ACF within the noise band of the argmin?) and supplies the rank-correlation input for H2.
  C3 — CycleNet with RCF module disabled (P=0 / no cycle token, same backbone, same everything else): the ablation isolating H3 (the cycle mechanism itself must pay off, so the P choice is not a free lunch on a useless module).
  C4 — Published CycleNet/other-paper numbers on the same dataset+horizon (external anchor): sanity-check that our implementation reproduces the ballpark; it does not participate in hypothesis tests.

4.5 Evaluation metrics
  MSE and MAE averaged over all forecast steps and variates (the standard CycleNet reporting); symmetric-MAPE as a secondary metric for M4 subsets. Report mean ± std across seeds. Each claim uses test-set metrics; C2/C3 use validation for early stopping and TEST for the reported comparison.

====================================================================
5. ANALYSIS PLAN
====================================================================
5.1 Head-to-head — ACF-P vs default-P (C1)
  For each dataset×horizon: difference Δ = MAE(P_default) − MAE(P_ACF) per seed. Paired test across seeds: with ≥5 seeds use paired t-test; with 3 seeds use Wilcoxon signed-rank (acknowledge low power) and, crucially, report the DIRECTIONAL CONSISTENCY (how many seeds show Δ>0) and effect size (mean relative error reduction %). Success = Δ ≥ 0 (tie or win) with ≥ 2/3 seeds consistent, or a significant paired test.

5.2 P-sweep landscape (C2)
  Plot/table MAE(P) across the sweep per dataset. Report:
   (i)   argmin P*_err and its noise band [best ± 1 SE(seeds)],
   (ii)  whether P_ACF ∈ band (success = within band, or P_ACF is the band's argmin),
   (iii) whether P_default also ∈ band (to characterise when ACF adds nothing because defaults already tie).

5.3 Rank-correlation check (the headline "ACF predicts optimality" metric)
  For each dataset: order sweep candidates by mean ACF magnitude (descending) and by test MAE (ascending) → Kendall's tau_b and Spearman rho between ACF-rank and error-rank (expect negative correlation: high ACF ⇒ low error). Aggregate tau across the M4 many-dataset family (one point per dataset) to gain statistical power. Positive/near-zero tau = the ACF signal does NOT track performance and the method fails.

5.4 Tie handling / noise band
  Because multiple P can be statistically tied, "optimal" is not a single point. Definition: the optimal set = {P : MAE(P) within band of argmin}. Success is that P_ACF belongs to this set. This avoids over-claiming when a 24-vs-168 choice does not change error; in that case we report that ACF and default agree within the band and the ranking is stable.

5.5 Attributing performance (C3)
  RCF-on(P_ACF) vs RCF-off on identical protocol: paired comparison as in 5.1. If the module gives ≤0 gain, the whole "optimal P" question is vacuous on that dataset and it is flagged rather than counted as evidence.

5.6 Interpretation output per dataset
  A small table: dataset | true/documented periods | P_ACF (with vote+magnitude ranking) | P_default | sweep argmin (band) | ACF∈band? | Δ vs default | tau_b | RCF-on vs off gain. A cross-dataset summary of S1–S4 closes the answer to the research question.

====================================================================
6. FEASIBILITY, RUNTIME AND FALLBACKS
====================================================================
6.1 Current environment reality
  /workspace is empty (only task.json); Python 3.14.4 system-only; NO numpy/scipy/pandas/torch installed; network disabled; CPU-only (224 cores), no GPU. Therefore the full experiment is NOT runnable as-is. Concrete prerequisites to actually execute: pip-installable scientific stack (numpy, scipy, torch, pandas) and the datasets (§2.2). These are provisioning items outside the design, stated as assumptions, not solved here.

6.2 Runtime & scaling budget (if provisioned on the 224-CPU node)
  Dominant cost is CycleNet training across the P-sweep × horizons × seeds.
  - Per run: ETTh1 L=336 H=96, ~8.6k train pts, batch 32, 30–60 epochs (early stop): roughly minutes on GPU / tens of minutes on 224 CPU threads if the model is the lean DLinear-backbone variant. Multiply by (datasets ~5) × (sweep ~10) × (horizons up to 4) × (seeds 3) → the FULL grid is heavy (hundreds of runs). Mitigations, applied cumulatively until in budget:
    a) Epoch cap 40 + early stopping; batch 64.
    b) 3 seeds for head-to-head/ablation, 1–2 seeds for the sweep landscape (sweep is used for argmin/noise-band plus tau, which tolerates single-seed estimates).
    c) Subsampling: for ECL/Weather train on a random ~50% variate subset (reports per-variate-pooled behaviour on a subset; flagged as a limitation).
    d) Limit horizons to {96, 336} for the sweep, add {192, 720} only for the head-to-head if budget allows.
  - ACF step is near-free (O(N·K) per series) and the synthetic recovery study is cheap — this part runs even without heavy compute.

6.3 Fallback: synthetic-only proof-of-concept (runnable with minimal deps)
  If provisioning of real data fails, the design degrades gracefully to a self-contained PoC that still answers the question's core logically:
  - Generate synthetic series with known P (§2.1), run §3 ACF detection, confirm recovery (S1). 
  - Replace real CycleNet with a cheap reference forecaster that depends explicitly on P (e.g., seasonal-naive: ŷ_{t+h} = x_{t+h−P}, and seasonal-auto: ŷ using lag-P differenced linear fit) to demonstrate that P chosen by ACF attains near-minimal error over a P-sweep (mirrors S2/S3 without training a neural net). This preserves the experimental LOGIC (ACF-picked P ≈ best P on held-out error) when GPUs/torch/data are unavailable; it is clearly labelled as a fallback proxy, not the full CycleNet result.

6.4 What is NOT claimed
  No experiment has been run; this document specifies the design, controls, metrics and decision rules such that executing it (under the provisioning in 6.1) would concretely answer the research question with pre-registered success criteria.

====================================================================
DECISION RULES SUMMARY (for later execution)
- H1 accepted if synthetic recovery rate ≥ 95%.
- H2 accepted per dataset if P_ACF ∈ noise band of sweep argmin AND Δ vs default ≥ 0 (majority of seeds consistent) AND tau_b < 0 with p<0.05 (aggregated for M4).
- H3 accepted if RCF-on beats RCF-off (paired test or ≥2/3 seeds positive) on at least the synthetic and one real dataset.
- Any dataset breaking an assumption (dominant seasonality, shared periodicity) is reported and excluded from aggregate success, not silently adjusted.

4.1 How P enters the model (Residual Cycle Forecasting, RCF)
  CycleNet (Lin et al., NeurIPS 2024) augments a backbone forecaster (e.g., a linear/DLinear head) with an RCF module that holds a LEARNABLE cycle token of length P shared across time steps (per variate for multivariate data). For time step t the model emits a cycle component ŷ^cycle_t = token[t mod P]; the backbone is trained on residuals y_t − ŷ^cycle_{t−P} (cycle-to-cycle differences); forecast = backbone residual output + cycle component. Consequences that constrain our design:
   - P must be a single fixed positive integer per dataset (one cycle token, one period). This is why §3 aggregates to one P per dataset rather than per series.
   - RCF needs the lag-P history within the receptive window: lookback L must satisfy L ≥ 2·P (else the model cannot reference the previous cycle for early in-window steps). With L=336 this caps P ≤ 168, which comfortably covers all daily/weekly periods in our data while ruling out unrealistically long P (e.g., yearly for hourly data).

4.2 Model protocol (fixed across all P variants so P is the ONLY variable)
  - Backbone: DLinear-style head (the CycleNet default) for a lean, CPU-friendly baseline; note that the same protocol generalises to any backbone.
  - Lookback L = 336; horizons H ∈ {96, 192, 336, 720} for ETT/ECL/Weather; {24, 48, 168} or the M4 short-term horizons for M4 subsets.
  - Optimiser: Adam, lr 1e-3 (cosine decay), batch 32, MSE loss, early stopping on validation loss (patience 10).
  - Data normalisation per variate (standardisation) identical across variants.
  - Seeds: 3 seeds minimum, up to 5 if budget allows, identical seeds across all P variants of the same dataset/horizon (enables paired tests).

4.3 P-sweep range (per dataset)
  Let p1 = top ACF candidate, p2..p5 = the rest. Sweep set = {max(1, p1−2)…p1+2} ∪ {p2..p5} ∪ {default P by data frequency} ∪ {known alternates, e.g., 24 AND 168 for hourly data}. Clamp any candidate P to ≤ L/2 (=168) to respect the L ≥ 2P RCF constraint. This yields ~8–12 P values per dataset. Rationale: the sweep builds the error-vs-P landscape on which "optimal" is operationally defined, and tests whether the ACF picks a point on/near its minimum.

4.4 Baselines and controls, each tied to a specific claim it isolates
  C1 — CycleNet(P_ACF) vs CycleNet(P_default): the core head-to-head for H2's "at least as good as convention". P_default = {24 hourly, 96 for 15-min, 144 for 10-min, 7 weekly, 12 monthly, 4 quarterly} (the paper's frequency heuristic).
  C2 — CycleNet(P) for every P in the sweep: the error-vs-P curve; isolates H2's "optimality" (is P_ACF within the noise band of the argmin?) and supplies the rank-correlation input for H2.
  C3 — CycleNet with RCF module disabled (P=0 / no cycle token, same backbone, same everything else): the ablation isolating H3 (the cycle mechanism itself must pay off, so the P choice is not a free lunch on a useless module).
  C4 — Published CycleNet/other-paper numbers on the same dataset+horizon (external anchor): sanity-check that our implementation reproduces the ballpark; it does not participate in hypothesis tests.

4.5 Evaluation metrics
  MSE and MAE averaged over all forecast steps and variates (the standard CycleNet reporting); symmetric-MAPE as a secondary metric for M4 subsets. Report mean ± std across seeds. Each claim uses test-set metrics; C2/C3 use validation for early stopping and TEST for the reported comparison.

5. ANALYSIS PLAN
====================================================================
5.1 Head-to-head — ACF-P vs default-P (C1)
  For each dataset×horizon: difference Δ = MAE(P_default) − MAE(P_ACF) per seed. Paired test across seeds: with ≥5 seeds use paired t-test; with 3 seeds use Wilcoxon signed-rank (acknowledge low power) and, crucially, report the DIRECTIONAL CONSISTENCY (how many seeds show Δ>0) and effect size (mean relative error reduction %). Success = Δ ≥ 0 (tie or win) with ≥ 2/3 seeds consistent, or a significant paired test.

5.2 P-sweep landscape (C2)
  Plot/table MAE(P) across the sweep per dataset. Report:
   (i)   argmin P*_err and its noise band [best ± 1 SE(seeds)],
   (ii)  whether P_ACF ∈ band (success = within band, or P_ACF is the band's argmin),
   (iii) whether P_default also ∈ band (to characterise when ACF adds nothing because defaults already tie).

5.3 Rank-correlation check (the headline "ACF predicts optimality" metric)
  For each dataset: order sweep candidates by mean ACF magnitude (descending) and by test MAE (ascending) → Kendall's tau_b and Spearman rho between ACF-rank and error-rank (expect negative correlation: high ACF ⇒ low error). Aggregate tau across the M4 many-dataset family (one point per dataset) to gain statistical power. Positive/near-zero tau = the ACF signal does NOT track performance and the method fails.

5.4 Tie handling / noise band
  Because multiple P can be statistically tied, "optimal" is not a single point. Definition: the optimal set = {P : MAE(P) within band of argmin}. Success is that P_ACF belongs to this set. This avoids over-claiming when a 24-vs-168 choice does not change error; in that case we report that ACF and default agree within the band and the ranking is stable.

5.5 Attributing performance (C3)
  RCF-on(P_ACF) vs RCF-off on identical protocol: paired comparison as in 5.1. If the module gives ≤0 gain, the whole "optimal P" question is vacuous on that dataset and it is flagged rather than counted as evidence.

5.6 Interpretation output per dataset
  A small table: dataset | true/documented periods | P_ACF (with vote+magnitude ranking) | P_default | sweep argmin (band) | ACF∈band? | Δ vs default | tau_b | RCF-on vs off gain. A cross-dataset summary of S1–S4 closes the answer to the research question.
